body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Cardiovascular events in the five years after hospitalisation for community-acquired pneumonia: a linked national cohort of 18,400 adults with matched controls","authors":"Lindqvist-Opoku S, Marchetti-Hale D, Tanaka-Boateng R","year":2018,"venue":"Caddisford Respiratory Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/jre.2018.0247","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 18,400 adults discharged after community-acquired pneumonia and 73,600 population controls matched on age, sex and area for five years using linked national data. The hazard ratio for a first myocardial infarction, stroke or heart failure admission was 1.9 in the first year and 1.3 in years two to five. Adjustment for cardiovascular disease and diabetes before the pneumonia reduced the later estimate to 1.15 (95 percent CI 1.07 to 1.24). Mortality was higher throughout. The authors note that frailty was not measured and that population controls were healthier than patients in ways the adjustment could not capture."},{"title":"Long-term mortality after community-acquired pneumonia compared with other acute infections: a registry study","authors":"Achebe-Carlsson P, Fenwick-Osei M","year":2020,"venue":"Infection Outcomes Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using a hospital infection registry, we compared five-year mortality of 6,200 adults discharged after community-acquired pneumonia with 9,100 adults discharged after urinary tract infection or cellulitis. Five-year mortality was 38 percent after pneumonia and 33 percent after the other infections. After adjustment for age, comorbidity and a frailty score, the hazard ratio was 1.12 (95 percent CI 1.04 to 1.20). The excess was concentrated in the first year. The authors argue that part of the apparent long-term effect of pneumonia seen against the general population reflects the frailty of people who are admitted with any infection."},{"title":"Choosing the comparison group in studies of outcomes after infection: general population versus hospitalised controls","authors":"Haddad-Mwangi L, Brennan-Sato K","year":2022,"venue":"Tamsford Epidemiologic Methods Letters","doi":"10.5555/eml.2022.0074","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the two usual comparison groups for studies of long-term outcomes after an infection admission. General population controls overstate the effect of the infection because admitted patients are frailer and sicker before the infection. Controls admitted with another infection understate it when that infection shares some of the same long-term effects. In three linked datasets, estimates against the two comparison groups bracketed the estimate from an analysis using each patient's own history before the infection. We recommend reporting results against both comparison groups and measuring frailty before the index admission."},{"title":"Frailty, pre-existing cardiovascular disease and long-term outcomes after pneumonia: a confounding analysis","authors":"Sorensen-Adeyemi J, Kowalczyk-Nnamdi E","year":2021,"venue":"Caddisford Respiratory Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/jre.2021.0119","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 9,600 adults discharged after pneumonia and matched population controls, we measured frailty with a hospital frailty score calculated from admissions in the two years before the pneumonia. Adjusting for this frailty score halved the excess five-year mortality, from a hazard ratio of 1.62 to 1.29, and reduced the excess of cardiovascular events from 1.34 to 1.14. Adjusting for complications during the pneumonia admission reduced the estimates further, but the authors warn that these complications lie on the causal path and should not be adjusted for in the main analysis."},{"title":"Moving into long-term care within two years after hospitalisation for pneumonia in adults aged 75 and over","authors":"Petrov-Lindgren A, Okafor-Whitlock B","year":2023,"venue":"Ageing and Health Services Research","doi":"10.5555/ahsr.2023.0156","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 4,300 adults aged 75 and over who lived at home before a pneumonia admission, 9 percent moved into long-term care within two years, against 4 percent of matched adults from the general population. The difference was largest among people with cognitive impairment and among those who lived alone. About half of the moves happened within three months of discharge. The authors suggest that loss of independence is a patient-important outcome that registries rarely capture and that care home entry can be identified from linked address and social care data."},{"title":"Linking pneumonia registries to national death and hospital admission data: completeness and pitfalls","authors":"Varga-Asante T, Holmberg-Iqbal N","year":2016,"venue":"Health Data Linkage Reports","doi":"10.5555/hdlr.2016.0032","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked a regional pneumonia registry to national death data and regional hospital admissions using deterministic and probabilistic methods. Linkage succeeded for 98.7 percent of registry patients. Causes of death on death certificates agreed with hospital diagnoses for cardiovascular deaths in 81 percent of cases. Admissions to hospitals outside the region were missed, affecting about 4 percent of patients who moved during follow-up. We recommend censoring at the date of leaving the region and using hospital diagnoses rather than death certificates alone to define cardiovascular events."}]}
